# Using the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1997 (NLSY97) metadata

These files describe the variables of National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1997 (NLSY97) (`nlsy97`). Use them to find variables, read their
question text, codes and missing codes, and see which waves and forms asked them.

## Steps

1. If you can run `pdt search` (below), search first: a subject, a scale signature or an
   `available` filter gives an exact, labeled list without reading any shard. Add `--names`
   when a result may be long.
2. Read `index.md` for the shards, their sizes and the labels they support.
3. Pick the shard that matches the question: a publisher subject, a group (battery, section),
   a scale signature, or the release/table shard for everything. Read its `.txt` form first.
   A release shard of a large dataset is far bigger than any one answer needs.
4. For codes, missing codes, full question text and per-wave availability, read the same
   variables in the shard's `.jsonl` form.
5. Answer with the completeness label (below), and cite the shard and filter you used.

## Completeness labels

Every list of variables you report must say how it was produced, with one of these labels.
The label describes the method, not your confidence. Don't upgrade it.

| Label | When to use it |
|---|---|
| `complete` | You report exactly the variables of one shard whose header says `complete`, or a filter `pdt search` labeled `complete`. |
| `complete_by_rule` | The same, for a shard or search labeled `complete_by_rule`. Name the rules and versions from its header. |
| `approximate` | Anything else: you searched text, used `topic` (annotation) shards, combined or pruned shards by judgment, or picked variables by reading them. |

Combining shards keeps the worst label among them only if the combination is itself a filter
(an AND or OR of the shards' filters); state that filter. If you drop or add any variable by
judgment, the result is `approximate`.

With every result, give what's needed to rerun it: the release(s) in scope, the number of
variables in scope, the filter (from the shard header), and the rule versions.

A `complete` result is complete with respect to the records in scope: if the repo covers
part of a release, say so, using the scope in the shard header. Subject shards are complete
with respect to the publisher's own subject list, which may miss items a reader would
consider on-topic; say so when it matters. If a subject shard and a group shard give the
same variables, report the stronger label (`complete`, then `complete_by_rule`, then
`approximate`) and cite that shard.

## Searching with code

If the shared library is installed, `pdt search PATH --filter '<json>'` runs a filter and
prints a labeled result, e.g. `--filter '{"subject": "Abortion"}'`. Filter keys: `release`,
`table`, `name`, `group`, `subject`, `topic`, `derived`, `available`, `waves`, `field`, `text`.
Several keys in one filter must all match. `waves` (a wave, a list, or
`{"from": A, "to": B}`) keeps variables asked in any of those waves.

A filter without `release` searches the current release (`1997-2023`); `--release all`
searches every release, so a variable kept across releases appears once per release.
`--names` prints only the names (one line, after the header); `--limit N --offset M` prints
one page. The header always gives the total `count`, the scope and the label, so a short
page of a `complete` result is still `complete`, provided you read every page.

Scale signatures name a response format by rule. Searching by one gives a
`complete_by_rule` list, and combining it with `available` or `waves` keeps that label:

    pdt search PATH --filter '{"derived": {"scale_signature": "yes_no"}, "available": {"wave": 2024}}'

Finding the same variables by text search or by reading gives the same list but is
`approximate`.

For a question about when or to whom a variable was asked ("every item on form A in 1988",
"thermometers asked in 1978"), use `available`, not your own reading of the shards:

    pdt search PATH --filter '{"available": {"wave": 1988, "form": "A"}}'
    pdt search PATH --filter '{"derived": {"scale_signature": "thermometer"}, "available": {"wave": 1978}}'

`available` matches a variable with an availability entry for that wave on that form, or with
no form (everyone in that wave was asked); leave out `form` for "asked at all in that wave".
`sample`, `mode`, `phase` and `geography` work the same way, when the dataset's
`dimensions` define them: `{"wave": 2022, "geography": "25"}` is "asked there in 2022".
It is `complete` when availability comes from the publisher or the data file. Picking the
same variables by reading a shard gives the same list but is `approximate`, because you made
the selection; if you can't run `pdt search`, say so and label it `approximate`.

## Rules

- Names are as the publisher spells them.
- Fields marked corrected (`*` in the line form, `view.corrected` in JSONL) differ from the
  source; mention the correction when you quote the text.
- Never treat an `approximate` source as complete: `topic` shards are annotations.
- These files are generated; don't edit them.

## About this dataset

From the repo's `AGENT_NOTES.md`.

*Written by Claude (PublicDataToolkit Task 69), 2026-11-20, from NLS's documentation and measurements on this slice.*

In the NLSY97, a person's answer about a given year, or at a given age, isn't always in one obvious round. This describes how NLS's data work and what NLS documents; which approach fits an analysis is the user's choice.

**Why answers spread.**
- **Rounds change frequency.** Rounds 1–15 were annual (1997–2011), rounds 16–21 every two years (2013–2023). Fielding "began in the fall of the survey year and continued through the spring of the following year" ([Interview Methods](https://nlsinfo.org/content/cohorts/nlsy97/intro-to-the-sample/interview-methods)).
- **People miss rounds and come back.** In this slice, 44% of respondents missed at least one round and were interviewed again, and 4.8% of pairs of consecutive interviews skip a round. A round in which a person wasn't interviewed has the code -5 (non-interview) in every variable, and RNI gives the reason.
- **Many questions ask about the time "since the date of last interview" (DLI).** So the reference period is each person's own, from their previous interview to this one. After a missed round it covers the gap: NLS collects "detailed retrospective information about work history, education, training, marital status, and fertility since the date of the respondent's last interview" ([Retention & Reasons for Non-Interview](https://nlsinfo.org/content/cohorts/nlsy97/intro-to-the-sample/retention-reasons-non-interview)).
- **Wording and universes change by round.** YSAQ-360C asks "since the last interview" through 2011 and "within the past twelve months" in 2013 and 2015. "Ever" questions (YSAQ-359, YSAQ-363) were asked of everyone in 1997, and later only of those who hadn't answered as of the last interview. In each record, `questions[].waves` and the universe by wave say which.

**What NLS recommends.**
- "Researchers analyzing topics where time periods are critical should carefully examine the reference period of the questions and the actual interview date for individual respondents" ([Interview Methods](https://nlsinfo.org/content/cohorts/nlsy97/intro-to-the-sample/interview-methods)).
- For the interview date, use CV_INTERVIEW_DATE~M and ~Y (rounds 2 on) or CV_INTERVIEW_CMONTH (continuous months, January 1980 = 1). For the date of the previous interview, find the round the respondent was last interviewed, then take that round's interview date (same page).
- For status at a point in time, NLS builds **event history arrays**: employment by week, marital and cohabitation status by month, program participation, schooling, arrests and incarceration. "Using these arrays, researchers can extract the status of a respondent at a point in time or over time." They run from age 14 (12 for arrests) to the last interview ([Codebook Supplement, Appendix 6](https://nlsinfo.org/content/cohorts/nlsy97/other-documentation/codebook-supplement/appendix-6-event-history-creation-and)).
- **Created variables** (CV_ and CVC_ names) resolve common cases: the age at interview (CV_AGE_INT_DATE), "the round in which the respondent was last interviewed" (CVC_RND), and cumulative versions across rounds (CVC_, "regardless of interview status") ([Created Variable Appendices](https://nlsinfo.org/node/411); the CV_HGC_EVER_EDT codebook note).

**In this repo.**
- `person_year` has one row per respondent and survey year, so a question's answers over time are one column.
- CV_INTERVIEW_CMONTH and CV_AGE_INT_DATE give each row's interview month and age. MAR_STATUS_YYYY.MM, in `person`, is NLS's monthly marital array (group `array-mar-status`).
- To find a person's answer about year Y or at age A, the options are:
  1. the round whose interview is at that age, from CV_AGE_INT_DATE. In this slice, 14–27% of people have no interview at a given age from 16 to 25, and about half at 30 and 35;
  2. the round or rounds whose reference period covers it, for a since-the-last-interview question: from the previous interview's CV_INTERVIEW_CMONTH to this one's. For YSAQ-360C, about half of people have two or more answers whose periods overlap a given year in 2005–2010, and with twelve-month questions in a two-year cycle, 80% of people have no answer whose period overlaps 2012;
  3. NLS's event history array, for the statuses it covers. In this slice, MAR_STATUS has a value for the month a person turned 25 for 94% of respondents, against 79% with at least one interview at age 25.
- `pdt diff . 1997-2023 --waves` lists each record's changes between rounds: wording, universe, codes.

**Finding the candidates with code: `pdt.panel`.**
- `Panel(repo, month_zero=(1979, 12)).answers(name, pubid, year=Y)` or `age=A` returns every round's answer that could be the one about year Y or at age A. Each comes with:
  - its round, interview month and age;
  - its reference period, taken from the wording's `reference_period`;
  - how many months of Y it covers, or how far its age is from A;
  - the universe that round.

  If there's none, it returns the reasons, such as "not interviewed (noninterview code 96)".
- **It never chooses.** `pick(candidates, policy)` does, with a policy you name: `exact`, `nearest`, `most_overlap` or `latest`. It reports a tie between disagreeing answers instead of breaking it, and keeps every candidate.
- `month_zero=(1979, 12)` is NLS's continuous-month scheme: January 1980 is month 1 (Codebook Supplement, Appendix 7).
- `scripts/panel_check.py` checks it against `scripts/measure_spread.py`: the counts agree for 2005, 2010 and 2012.

```python
from pdt.panel import Panel, pick
p = Panel("~/pdt-nlsy97", month_zero=(1979, 12))
cands = p.answers("YSAQ-360C", 1, year=2005)      # 2005 round: 11 months of 2005; 2006 round: 1 month
pick(cands, "most_overlap").answer.wave          # 2005, because the policy says so
```
